claims.text: Processing techniques can significantly improve the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy relative to its as-cast state.
Processing can improve the hardness of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
Processing can improve the elastic modulus of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
Processing can increase the yield strength of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy by 10–20% relative to the as-cast state.
Processing can increase the ultimate tensile strength of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy by 15–30% relative to the as-cast state.
Nanoindentation and uniaxial tensile testing can be used to evaluate the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
The proposed nanoindentation depth range is 100–1000 nm.
The proposed tensile strain-rate range is 10^-3–10^-1 s^-1.
The proposed testing-temperature range is room temperature to 800°C.
Grain refinement and precipitation of secondary phases mediate the proposed improvement in mechanical properties.
An increase in dislocation density contributes to strengthening of the alloy.
Grain-boundary strengthening contributes to the improved mechanical properties.
Hot isostatic pressing or forging may alter the microstructure and mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
The magnitude of mechanical-property improvement depends on the processing technique and processing conditions.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing as-cast and processed FeNiCrMn specimens using nanoindentation and uniaxial tensile testing.
Failure of processed FeNiCrMn to show a significant mechanical-property improvement over the as-cast state would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes improvement and microstructural mediation to processing, but the stated intervention consists only of mechanical testing. Nanoindentation and tensile testing characterize properties and do not, as specified, implement the processing needed to produce grain refinement or secondary-phase precipitation.
